newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-Light seen at end of Sappi tunnel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Light seen at end of Sappi tunnel.

text.p: After posting dismal half year earnings South African pulp and paper producer Sappi Ltd has hit bottom and should now start to catch an expected upturn in the notoriously cyclical industry, analysts said on Monday.
Earlier the firm posted six month earnings per share of just 16 cents, towards the bottom of market expectations and a steep fall from the 215 cents last year.
The firm also scrapped its dividend for the period as low prices bit a huge chunk out of its bottom line.
However, analysts now believe the worst is out of the way and they were picking through the firm's results statement for hints of better times to come. They were not disappointed.
"There is good news about price increases," said Mark Rule, analyst at SocGen Frankel Pollack.

The firm said most major suppliers had announced price increases in recent months that would be effective from May and -- unlike attempts to push through rises earlier in the year -- these rises were being accepted by the market.

The firm also said the key North American market looked as if it would be riding the crest of the long-awaited upturn in the cycle. Sappi said demand there was strong and prices were now on an upwards trend with coated free paper prices rising by $80 per short ton on June 1.
"Prices have certainly bottomed out. Looking forward things should be largely positive from here on," said Paul Carter, analyst at ING Barings.
Sappi, whilst admitting that last year's total earnings figure is not going to be matched this time around, did say the second half of the current year is expected to be better than the first.
Analysts agreed. "The second half will be much better and next year will be better again," said one analyst who declined to be named.

Europe, however, is not as rosy a picture as North America. The rate of price increases there is being restrained by currency fluctuations and additional paper capacity, but a rise in pulp prices is set to at least support current levels, the firm said, confirming the industry view.

On May 20 Finnish forestry group Enso said there had been a clear, though cautious, upturn in pulp prices that could support an uplift in paper prices. On the same day Sweden's AB Kinnevik said pulp inventory holdings were falling, giving scope for pulp increases later in the year.

Sappi's share price dipped on the earnings news, dropping two rand to 39.00 before coming back to 40.00 at 0850 GMT. Ratings agency Duff & Phelps Ratings Co also put the firm on a negative credit watch.
However, analysts said the share price fall was largely unwarranted and could be due to a short-term negative reaction
